title: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan

sections.title: Process Overview
sections.text:
16.1 Process Overview
In this section, we’ll provide details to help you comprehend the actual steps involved
in undertaking the FMEA initiative.

sections.title: Action Plan
sections.text:
16.1.1 Action Plan
Companies can take the following 10 steps to chart a step-by-step approach to develop-
ing an action plan using FMEA. With the exception of the first step, all the following
steps are mapped in the SAP system:
1. Review existing business processes.
Examine how each component of the process functions and its relation to the other
items. For example, what process is currently in place to receive hazardous materials
from a supplier, or which packing material does the company use to pack its fragile
products? Use a detailed flowchart for each business process to review the chain of
processes. When you review each component of the process with your team mem-
bers, everyone gains a greater understanding of the entire process and how the var-
ious components are interlinked. Using the process flowchart, you can assign
applicable components to the relevant process owners who are performing specific
functions in different departments of the company. Assigning applicable compo-
nents to relevant process owners ensures accountability and visibility by clearly seg-
regating and identifying their roles and responsibilities in the FMEA initiative.
2. List potential failure modes.
List all the possible ways a product or process can fail to perform its function. Refer
to previous documentation and other records to gain insight into the nature of pre-
vious problems and how these were handled.
3. List potential effects of failure.
Make detailed notes about the potential effects of failure. The effect directly relates
to the failure of the specific process or component to perform its function. While
noting details, record how the failure would affect other interconnected processes
and functions.
© 

691
16.1 Process Overview
4. Assign severity rankings to each effect.
Rank each effect based on how it would impact the entire value chain. This value
chain can be a customer, dependent subsequent operations, or people involved in
operating the process. The severity ranking is based on a relative scale ranging from
1 to 10, with 1 being extremely low and 10 being the highest severity. When assign-
ing a severity to each effect, you can begin with a standard, general scale and then
work closely with other team members to define a specific and relevant severity
ranking for each effect.
5. Assign occurrence rankings to each cause.
The occurrence ranking reflects the frequency or likelihood that a cause or failure
mechanism will occur. Just like severity ranking, the occurrence ranking is also
based on a scale of 1 to 10. Review the occurrence frequency by referring to the data
and reports, such as the equipment failure record, customer complaints, or even
the repair and rework reports.
6. Assign rankings to failure detection.
Identify each process- or product-related control in place, evaluate the process of
detecting failure, and assign a detection ranking to a failure on a scale of 1 to 10. A
detection ranking of 1 indicates that detecting failure is certain, and a detection
ranking of 10 means that detection of a failure isn’t possible or that no checks or
controls are in place to detect the failure.
7. Calculate the RPN.
As directed by the business process owner, the system automatically calculates the
RPN, which quantifies the amount of risk of failure and helps prioritize improve-
ment efforts. The RPN is determined by multiplying severity, occurrence, and
detection. It’s always in the range of 1 to 1,000. The higher the RPN, the greater the
risk.
8. Develop an action plan to reduce RPN.
Lowering the RPN is made possible by focusing on lowering one or more of its three
factors (severity, occurrence, or detection). For example, a reduction in detection
ranking is accomplished by adding fail-safe processes in shutdowns, installing
alarms or sensors, or ensuring timely preventive maintenance.
9. Implement the action plan.
Assign people to each action and finalize a timeline for the completion of actions. A
practical approach to adopt is the “who, what, and when” approach to implement
the action plan.
10. Recalculate the resulting RPN.
Recalculate the RPN after implementing the action plan to determine whether the
desired RPN has been achieved. If it hasn’t, it may be necessary to repeat this series
of steps or perhaps develop a new action plan.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
692

sections.title: Failure Across Categories
sections.text:
16.1.2 Failure Across Categories
FMEA categorizes risk of failure across three categories, including occurrence (how
likely failure is to occur), severity (how big an impact it would have), and detection (how
likely the failure is to be detected as soon as it occurs):
Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection
FMEA uses a 1–10 ranking for each factor, with 10 being very likely to occur, have a sig-
nificant impact, or be detected. FMEA multiplies the three individual rankings of those
three factors to come up with the RPN. The value of the RPN can be in the range of 1 to
1,000. The higher the RPN value is, the greater the possibility of failure is in a produc-
tion or business process. Companies must then reduce the RPN as much as possible to
prevent or eliminate failures. Companies can use FMEA in the SAP S/4HANA system to
lower their RPNs by taking preventative and detection measures.
The team that manages the FMEA predefines the valuation (on a scale of 1 to 10) for
each of the three areas mentioned (occurrence, detection, and prevention) and the RPN
benchmark that it wants to achieve. The FMEA team then undertakes practical actions,
such as making design changes, placing visual signboards, and pasting labels to edu-
cate the production or process users to adhere to given guidelines or conduct technical
skills enhancement trainings. After performing these actions, the FMEA team updates
the valuation of each of the three areas, and the system automatically recalculates the
RPN. If the RPN is reduced to the benchmark level, the FMEA team calls this achieve-
ment a success. If not, another round of practical actions is put in place, and the process
to calculate new or reduced RPNs starts all over again.

sections.title: Closed-Loop Quality Approach
sections.text:
16.1.3 Closed-Loop Quality Approach
The ability to create FMEA along with all its components and then integrate it with con-
trols in the SAP system provides the added leverage of having all the critical informa-
tion in one system (the SAP system). Further, FMEA also provides an option to create an
extensive question list that acts as a validation tool to ensure that all questions were
eventually validated with the correct/desired answers, and then it becomes possible for
a company to achieve a reduced RPN.
Figure 16.1 shows a step-by-step FMEA approach 1 in closed-loop quality management.
It’s the direct outcome of complaints coming from customers 2 or analytics such as
statistical process control monitoring 3 in production processes.
Finally, you can leverage FMEA to incorporate important characteristics in an inspec-
tion plan 4 for regular and consistent monitoring and control of characteristics that
are critical to quality.
Now that you have a better understanding of what FMEA is and does, let’s move on to
setting up FMEA in the system.

3 The Worklist shows the FMEAs or other objects that you’ve worked on in the recent

4 The cross-linking area helps to bring together all the FMEA items in one work area so

Tips and Tricks
We’ll be taking the longer route of explaining each and every FMEA item in this chapter

After reading the entire chapter and understanding all FMEA items, we suggest that

these productivity tools.
Choose the New icon in Figure 16.4, and from the dropdown, you can create a new

created FMEA or question list that you can use to save time and effort instead of man-
ually entering all the details all over again.
Figure 16.4 FMEA Cockpit to Create a New FMEA
Choose FMEA from the dropdown list in Figure 16.4, and the system brings up the basic
data view of the FMEA in Figure 16.5. On the right side of the screen, enter “REVO” for

the FMEA field (for the rest of this chapter, we’ll use FMEA REVO as an example) and
enter its Description. Notice the additional icons right next to the FMEA field that
enable you to add additional notes or attachments for reference and record purposes.
Figure 16.5 Basic Data Tab of FMEA
The option to attach documents or notes is also generally available while you’re creat-
ing all items of the FMEA. The system prompts you to select the FMEA type, which can
be either System FMEA Product or System FMEA Process. Select the Product option, and
enter material number “FG129”. Enter the planned start and end dates of FMEA in the
lower half of the screen (not shown). When you’ve actually started and then finally

in the bottom half of Figure 16.5 (not shown).
Choose the Texts tab to reach the screen shown in Figure 16.6. Here, you incorporate
more details about the FMEA, including adding an FMEA description and notes. You
can even upload (and download) the content from some other data source, such as
another drive in your laptop, and incorporate it in either the description or the note
areas of the FMEA. This is possible when you choose the relevant upload or download
icons.
In the Participant(s) tab, enter the roles and names of the persons who will be part of
the FMEA team. This step enables you to assign responsibility to the relevant persons.
Then, in all subsequent status updates or reporting, information on participants helps
you find whose tasks are pending or overdue, or even which resource/participant is
assigned what task(s).

Tips and Tricks
Use Transaction BP in SAP S/4HANA to create or amend business partners (team mem-
bers) who will be part of the FMEA initiative.
In the Result tab (see Figure 16.7), you can see that while you’re creating a new FMEA,
the system hasn’t calculated the FMEA results (the RPN). Later, you’ll see how the sys-

Figure 16.7 Results Tab of FMEA
In the lower half of the screen, in the Valuation Specifications area, the system enables

For this example, use the valuation procedure to calculate the RPN. In addition, it’s

important to note that you can define the minimum result that the system must

Assesst. (assessment) to declare the FMEA initiative a success or a failure.
Save the FMEA by choosing the Save button located in the bottom-right side of the

Note
You can click to the Message icon located at the top-right side of Figure 16.7 to view any

Figure 16.7 shows that we’ve created and saved FMEA REVO. In case of a warning or

Note
As FMEA is a specialized audit management tool, it’s possible to configure the levels of
audit components as well as set other control functions, including how to structure

Let’s now create the FMEA items, including a function list.

sections.title: Create Function List
sections.text:
16.2.1 Create Function List
To create a function list, right-click FMEA REVO, and the system brings up the option to
create a function list (Figure 16.8). Select Functions, and the system brings up the screen
shown in Figure 16.9.
In FMEA, a function list consists of a list of FMEA items that are further broken down
into individual components. It consists of characteristics, their associated failure
modes, and the reasons for their occurrence. We’ll cover all of them in the following
sections of this chapter.
Tips and Tricks
You can always perform a consistency check for FMEA by using the available options
available.
© 

699
16.2 Set Up
On the right side of Figure 16.9, enter a function list and a short description. In addition,
enter relevant text in the Definition area. All of this entered text will eventually be visi-
ble in either FMEA or its print preview, which we’ll cover later. As soon as we enter these
texts, the system automatically updates this information on the left side of Figure 16.9.
Hence, while you continue entering or updating information on the right side of the
screen, the system keeps updating it on the left side. Notice that there is a display field
for RPN Value, which at this stage is zero because the RPN isn’t calculated yet.
Figure 16.8 Creating Functions
Figure 16.9 Basic Data of Function List

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
700
Tips and Tricks
If you don’t want to manually enter identification details in FMEA items, such as in the
Functions field in Figure 16.9, then leave it blank. The system automatically assigns an
internal numeric identification to all such FMEA items for which it’s unable to find
identification. However, you do still have to enter a description of each FMEA item.
Choose Valuation Specifications in Figure 16.9, and the system brings up Figure 16.10,
showing the Valuation Specifications of the function list. Here again, because of the
correct configuration in place, the system automatically selects RPN calculation as the
valuation procedure.
In the Catalogs area, enter the Catalog Profile “000000001”, which consists of an indi-
vidual catalog and code group. A catalog, together with the code group, enables the pro-
cess owner to group or combine similar codes and information within a catalog. For
example, the Defect Types catalog lists out all the possible defects that one can encoun-
ter in FMEA, and each individual defect is denoted by its defect code. These individual
codes are grouped together as a code group: all electrical defects are grouped under one
code group, while all mechanical defects are combined in another code group.
For ease of understanding and working, we incorporate all the code groups applicable
in FMEA. For example, the Causes item has code group 5, so we incorporate it here.
Figure 16.10 Valuation Specifications of the Function List

16.2 Set Up
Note
You can use Transaction QS41 to add or amend any codes or code groups to meet your
business needs. Chapter 3 covers how to create a catalog profile and all the associated
catalogs, code groups, codes, and selected sets.

sections.title: Create Prerequisite
sections.text:
16.2.3 Create Prerequisite
A prerequisite is a precondition that the process owner must ensure before the start of
FMEA. For example, a kickoff meeting takes place to announce the formal start of the
FMEA initiative, or the process owners must first be trained and educated on the need
to use FMEA to bring about process improvements.
In Figure 16.14, right-click Function (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing avail-
able options, choose Prerequisite and then navigate to creating a new prerequisite.
On the right side of Figure 16.15, enter the prerequisite, its description, and similar
details in the large text box.
© 

703
16.2 Set Up
Figure 16.14 Creating a Prerequisite
Figure 16.15 Basic Data Characteristic

sections.title: Creating a Characteristic
sections.text:
16.2.4 Creating a Characteristic
A characteristic is the individual business process that you want to monitor for
improvement within FMEA. It can be a physical or chemical property within a product
or a process step within the series of business process steps.
Back in Figure 16.11, right-click Functions (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing
options, choose the characteristic, and then navigate to create a new characteristic
(Figure 16.16). Enter the characteristic as “CHAR: Brake Pad” because we need to moni-
tor the diameter of the brake pad to see whether it has a material defect or there is some
other fault. Enter short text, and then from the dropdown list, select the Char. (charac-
teristic) Type as Process Characteristic. The other available option is Product Character-
istic. Select the characteristic Weighing as Critical characteristic to denote that it
contributes significantly to an automobile’s safety.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
704
Figure 16.16 Basic Data Tab of Characteristic
In the lower half of the screen (see Figure 16.17), enter the master inspection character-
istic (Master IC) as “Char: Brake Pad” and its Plant as “1710” so that the system can inte-
grate the FMEA characteristic with QM’s master inspection characteristics (see Figure
16.17). The importance of this integration will become evident when we create a control
plan in Section 16.7.
Figure 16.17 Lower Half of Basic Data Tab of Characteristic

sections.title: Create Failure Mode
sections.text:
16.2.5 Create Failure Mode
A failure mode is a physical or business process flaw or a defect that requires prevention
or correction to increase product or process reliability. In Figure 16.14 shown earlier,
right-click Function (on the left side of the screen). In the ensuing available options,
choose Failure Mode to create a new defect.
© 

705
16.2 Set Up
In Figure 16.18, create a new defect called “FM: BP JAMMING”, and enter short and long
descriptions. Figure 16.18 shows only the partial upper view of the item defect; when
you scroll down, you’ll see the screen in Figure 16.19.
Figure 16.18 Basic Data View of Defect (1/2)
Figure 16.19 enables you to enter the severity as a result of this error. The severity is con-
figured on a scale of 1 to 10. The higher the severity is, the greater the number should be.
From the dropdown for severity, select 10, which is for Extremely Severe Error (not shown,
but located further down the same screen), to denote that brake pad jamming (character-
istic) as a defect in an automobile is fatal (extreme severity) and must be promptly
addressed. Notice that fields such as Effect and Cause are blank at this stage. This is
because we still haven’t created these important FMEA items yet. As soon as we create
these FMEA items, the system automatically fills these fields with relevant information.
Figure 16.19 Basic Data View of Defect (2/2)
Figure 16.20 shows that the system calculates RPN when all FMEA items are in place. In
the Valuation area (not shown, but located further down the same screen), the system
uses the valuation profile Severity, followed by the valuation proposal, which we man-
ually select as a fatal error (the same as in Figure 16.19). The difference between Figure

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
706
16.19 and Figure 16.20 is that in the latter, you enter the specification you want to use as
a benchmark to monitor severity, whereas in the former, it’s the actual valuation that
results from the FMEA initiative as shown in the RPN Value area in Figure 16.19.
Figure 16.20 Valuation Specifications of Defect
The next step in the FMEA setup is to define the cause that leads to the defect.

sections.title: Create Cause
sections.text:
16.2.6 Create Cause
A cause is the reason or circumstances that leads to the defect in a product or process.
A cause can be a mechanical fault, an operator fault, noncalibrated equipment, or insuf-
ficient checks and balances in place to identify and correct a defect.
Figure 16.21 Creating Cause
© 

707
16.2 Set Up
In Figure 16.21, select the cause by right-clicking the defect (on the left side of the
screen). In the resulting options, choose Create  Cause.
In Figure 16.22, create a new cause called “CAUSE: CALIBRATION” and enter short and
long descriptions for it. In the valuation area, define the chances or the probability of
occurrence of this cause. For example, due to infrequent maintenance of brake pad
alignment equipment, the machine misfits the brake pad, leading to brake pad jam-
ming.
Figure 16.22 Basic Data of Cause
In the Valuation area, enter the actual valuation of the cause and the probability of its
occurrence. This is then used in the calculation of RPN. A probability of a cause occurring

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
708
only sometimes may have a valuation of 5. The system refers to this value from the val-
uation profile, where it’s already defined. Choose the Valuation Specifications tab in
Figure 16.22, and Figure 16.23 appears.
In Figure 16.22, the system will calculate the RPN when all FMEA items are in place. In
the Valuation area, the system uses Valuation Profile 8000 Probability of Occurrence,
followed by the valuation proposal that we manually select as 5 Moderate (the same as
in Figure 16.22). The difference between Figure 16.22 and Figure 16.23 is that in the latter,
you enter the specification that you want to use as a benchmark to monitor the proba-
bility of occurrence, whereas in the former, it’s the actual valuation that results from
your FMEA initiative. In principle, the actual valuation from the FMEA initiative should
be equal to or lower than the valuation specifications.
Figure 16.23 Valuation Specifications of Cause
With a characteristic’s defect and cause already in place in FMEA, the next step is to
define the preventive action that you’re going to put in place so that the defect ideally
doesn’t occur or is at least minimized.
Tips and Tricks
FMEA also completely integrates with quality notifications (see Chapter 12). Figure
16.24 shows an example of how you can load the objects from a quality notification
into FMEA. Figure 16.24 shows Notification 200000010, wherein you can choose the
Cause as Missing Component by selecting the available checkbox.
Note
The option to load notification objects is available when you’re creating relevant FMEA
items. Refer to Figure 16.21 and see From Notification Objects, which you can use to
integrate a cause from notification Figure 16.24 into FMEA.
© 

709
16.2 Set Up
Figure 16.24 Quality Notification Integration with FMEA

sections.title: Create Preventive Action
sections.text:
16.2.7 Create Preventive Action
A preventive action defines the preventive measure that the FMEA team puts in place
to ensure reduction or elimination of the cause of the defect. Figure 16.25 shows how to
create a preventive action for a cause.
Figure 16.25 Create Preventive Action

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
710
Right-click the cause on the left side of the screen. In the ensuing popup, select Create 
Preventive Action, and Figure 16.26 appears.
Figure 16.26 Basic Data of Preventive Action
Here, enter the preventive action, such as “REGULAR AND TIMELY CAL.”, and then
enter the dates during which this preventive action is to take place. In the Valuation
area of Figure 16.26, we select the Tgt (target) Valuation as 2 Very Low, which we expect
to achieve after the preventive action is ensured. This compares with current/previous
valuation of 5 Moderately high. During RPN calculation, the system looks for the target
valuation, which in this case is 2, as one of the three factors that calculates RPN. Here,
select the Occurrence item (not shown, but located down the same screen), which the
system uses to calculate RPN.
Choose the Status tab in Figure 16.26, and Figure 16.27 appears. Here, the system assigns
the system status of preventive action as Created. Later, we’ll show in the FMEA busi-
ness process how to update this system status once you’ve actually performed the pre-
ventive action and if you’ve been able to achieve the target valuation.
The next step in creating FMEA is to create a detection action that’s in direct relation to
the preventive action just created.
© 

711
16.2 Set Up
Figure 16.27 Status Tab of Preventive Action

sections.title: Create Detection Action
sections.text:
16.2.8 Create Detection Action
A detection action stipulates the possibility of detecting a defect or a failure mode. It
can range from quick and easy to detect a defect by putting the right tools in place to
nearly impossible to detect a defect.
This time, in Figure 16.25, right-click the cause (on the left side of the figure), and in the
ensuing options, select the option to create a detection action. The Detection Action
screen appears, as shown in Figure 16.28.
Figure 16.28 Basic Data of Detection Action

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
712
Enter the identification “DETECT: INSTALL SENSORS”, followed by its description. Enter
the Planned Start Date and To Be Completed By date of the detection action, and set the
Tgt. (target) Valuation of this detection action to 4 High (greater than or equal to
99.9%). It’s important to add here that the system uses the detection results (probabil-
ity of detection) to calculate RPN.
Finally, the last item of FMEA setup is to create an effect.

sections.title: Create an Effect
sections.text:
16.2.9 Create an Effect
An effect essentially reflects the damage or loss that results due to the defect in the
product or process. To create a new effect for a defect, see Figure 16.29. Right-click Fail-
ure Mode: Brake Pad Jamming. In the ensuing popup option, select Create  Effect.
Figure 16.29 Create Effect
In Figure 16.30, enter “FATAL CRASH” for the effect and enter its short and long descrip-
tions (not shown, but located on the same screen). Choose the Valuation Specifications
tab to enter the benchmark value for the effect or severity of this defect on the product
or process. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 16.31.
Figure 16.31 shows the Valuatn Profile of the effect or severity of a defect. Severity is the
third and final factor that the system uses in automatically calculating the RPN. In the
Valuation Specifications tab, you can specify the ideal or acceptable severity level that
the product or process can tolerate. Needless to say, a lower severity results in a lower
RPN and thus higher product safety and reliability. Save your entries.
© 

713
16.2 Set Up
Figure 16.30 Basic Data of Effect
Figure 16.31 Valuation Specifications Tab of Effect
Setting up FMEA in the QM area of SAP S/4HANA entails a lot of steps, including several
interdependent steps. Figure 16.32 shows the FMEA structure at a glance for this exam-
ple, REVO, and shows how the different FMEA items relate to each other.
With this, all the items that you need to create for FMEA are in place. To show you how
all the information that we entered so far appears in FMEA, either as a printout or print
preview, select REVO in the FMEA field on the left side of Figure 16.33, and then select
the Form button.
Here, you see that all the information we entered in various items of FMEA eventually
becomes available. Notice that the system hasn’t calculated the RPN yet.

sections.title: Business Processes
sections.text:
16.3 Business Processes
The business processes in FMEA entail a few important steps that will then form the
basis for the system to calculate RPN. These steps are as follows:
 Valuation of detection action
 Valuation of preventive action
 Valuation of effect
 Calculation of RPN
In each of these steps, the process owner specifies the actions taken to detect failure
and how this results in achieving the target or desired valuation of the item. In other
words, now you can start to fill in the actual and factual information and results in the
system after performing the necessary steps to detect failures in products or processes.
In the following sections, we’ll discuss each of these steps, before ending with some
additional FMEA features that don’t fit into any of the earlier categories.
© 

715
16.3 Business Processes

sections.title: Valuation of Detection Action
sections.text:
16.3.1 Valuation of Detection Action
Refer again to Figure 16.28, which shows the screen for detection action and is basically
the same screen that we were setting up in FMEA (Section 16.2.8). Notice that at the very
bottom of the figure, the Start Action checkbox isn’t selected, which means that no
detection action has taken place so far. We’ll cover this next.
In Figure 16.34 1, you can start the first step of the FMEA business process by entering
the actual start and end dates of detection action. This should be the actual start and
end dates when detection action, such as installing sensors, was ensured. You can also
enter the Level of Completion of detection action as a percentage (100%). Scroll down
the screen, and you’ll see the Status area 2.
Figure 16.34 Status Area of Detection Action
In Figure 16.34 2, the default or the current system status is Created, to denote that no
detection action has so far been initiated. Choose the Initial Action checkbox to signal
the start of detection action, followed by clicking the Open icon 2. On doing so, the sys-
tem updates the status to Outstanding 3. As soon as you perform any action, the sys-
tem correspondingly updates the status that you can see in the Status tab. The system
keeps updating the system status to match the last or latest action performed.
Next, update your detection action by choosing the Confirm icon on the right 3.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan

Choose the Status tab 1, and Figure 16.35 appears. This screen shows the last performed
action or status set as Confirmed. Hence, as the business process owner, keep setting
the actual status of the FMEA item (in this case, detection action) to reflect the actual
status of an action. It’s important to add here that the business process owner can use
the FMEA Monitor to see the statuses of various FMEAs for evaluation and possible
action, if necessary. We cover the FMEA Monitor later in Section 16.5.
Figure 16.35 Status Tab of Detection Action
Choose Set in Figure 16.35, which leads to the screen shown in Figure 16.36. Set the sys-
tem status to Complete to signal completion of detection action. Notice some of the
statuses available on this screen, including Remove to delete a status that has previ-
ously been set or Force Completion to force completion of a detection action when in
reality it wasn’t ensured.
Figure 16.36 Setting the System Status for the Detection Action in the Status Tab

status as Completed. Save your entries.

16.3.2 Valuation of Preventive Action
Repeat all the steps for preventive action (refer to Figure 16.26) that we just performed
for valuation of detection action. Once you’ve completed all steps for preventive
action, set the status to Completed.
The last step in the FMEA business process before the system is able to calculate RPN is
to enter the valuation of the effect of the defect.

sections.title: Valuation of Effect
sections.text:
16.3.3 Valuation of Effect
On confirming in FMEA that you’ve performed the necessary detective and preventive
actions to eliminate or reduce the occurrence of a defect in a product or process, the
final step is to enter a valuation of how these two actions have (positively) affected the
RPN by reducing it.
But before we cover valuation of effect on RPN, choose Cause: Machine Calibration (on
the left side of FMEA REVO), and then click on the Basic Data tab of the cause to bring
up the screen in Figure 16.38.
Figure 16.38 shows two of the three factors that make up the RPN: occurrence and
detection. Here, after we perform valuations of prevention and detection actions, the
system has assigned a valuation of 2.0 to occurrence and 4.0 to detection. In addition,
notice that the system still hasn’t calculated the RPN Value yet; it will only be able to do
so when the third and final factor, which is effect or severity, is valuated.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
718
Figure 16.38 Probabilities of Occurrence and Detection Updated in the Cause of FMEA
Choose Effect located on the left side of Figure 16.38 (not shown), and the screen in
Figure 16.39 appears. Select the Severity as 10 Extremely Serious Error to denote that the
effect of this defect still remains high.
Figure 16.39 Basic Data Tab of Effect without RPN
Next, we’ll show how the system automatically calculates RPN.

sections.title: Calculation of Risk Priority Number
sections.text:
16.3.4 Calculation of Risk Priority Number
In Figure 16.40, we chose FMEA REVO and then the Result tab. The Overall Assesst.
(assessment) reflects that FMEA REVO isn’t assessed yet, nor are FMEA results calcu-
lated (Result Calcul.).
In the Valuation Specifications area, for Procedure, choose 81 Calculation of Action Pri-
ority (AP) and Risk Priority Number (RPN), and then select Rating Profile 81 Rating: No
Risk, Medium Risk, High Risk. Finally, select the minimum result that the RPN must
reach to declare the preventive and detection actions as successful (in this example, it’s
80.0).
Choose the Valuate button in Figure 16.40, and this leads to the screen shown in Figure
16.41. Here, the system calculates the FMEA result (Result Calcul.) as 80.0 via the follow-
ing formula:
Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection
RPN = 10 × 2 × 4 = 80.0
Figure 16.40 FMEA before Valuation

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
720
Figure 16.41 Result Tab of FMEA with Automatic RPN Calculation
Notice that the system assigns the rating as 01 No Risk and the Overall Assesst. (assess-
ment) as 1 Passed. To gain a better understanding of how the system assigned 01 No
Risk and the role the rating profile has in this, refer to Section 16.8.6.
Figure 16.42 Status after Executing Valuation
© 

721
16.3 Business Processes
Choose the Status tab in Figure 16.41, and the screen shown in Figure 16.42 appears,
which reflects the sequence of steps undertaken for FMEA, including Valuation Exe-
cuted.
Tips and Tricks
As in this example, the FMEA rating was successful: the results met the specification of
80.0. Had the FMEA been less than 80.0, the system would have brought up a provision
to manually overwrite the system-calculated RPN FMEA results. This option is espe-
cially helpful when the difference between system-calculated FMEA results is very
close to the target value and isn’t worth the time, effort, or resources to conduct
another round of FMEA-related activities.

sections.title: Question List
sections.text:
16.4 Question List
During the FMEA initiative, one of the critical components is the availability of a ques-
tion list. A question list is a list of questions that the users or business process owners
answer to ensure complete traceability and accountability. You create a question list
after creating an FMEA in the system. Further, you also need to ensure that the ques-
tion list is approved before the users can update the answers to the questions con-
tained in the question list. Here again, the system provides the flexibility to copy a new
question list from an existing one (template), as well as upload it from external sources.
You can also assign a question list to FMEA.

sections.title: Create Questions in the Question List

16.4.1 Create Questions in the Question List

as a description. You can also assign a validity to the question list. The functions of
Texts and Contact Person are the same as we previously covered for FMEA, so we won’t
repeat them here.
Choose Valuation Specs in Figure 16.50, which leads to Figure 16.51, where you assign
the procedures to calculate the valuation. Further, you can also assign a priority to the
question list to reflect its importance. In the Valuation area (not shown), you assign a

Lastly, you can import documents from your local hard drive so that you don’t have to
create them all in FMEA.

sections.title: Risk Analysis
sections.text:
16.6 Risk Analysis
You can search for relevant FMEAs or their items from many search criteria, such as
dates, status of the FMEA, or person(s) who created or changed the FMEA. For this
example, select the FMEA radio button and then, in the Identification field, enter
“REVO”. Finally, choose Execute (not shown, but located at the bottom-right side of the
screen). This leads to Figure 16.57.
Figure 16.57 shows all the previously entered (or calculated) details, including the RPN
result of 80.0, the FMEA type (process), and the dates when it was first created and then
subsequently changed. With many icons available, you can add new fields, change lay-
outs, or even create a printout of the report on FMEA components.
Figure 16.57 Detailed View of the FMEA Monitor
16.6 Risk Analysis
You can run a risk analysis for the causes in an FMEA based on detection actions, pre-
ventive actions, and the severity of defects, and then represent the risk using risk
matrixes. You can start the risk analysis for one or more FMEAs from the FMEA Moni-
tor (Figure 16.57) and from the FMEA Cockpit. The risk analysis shows an overview of the
risk situation, based on the specified FMEAs and using risk matrixes. It takes all causes
of the specified FMEAs into account and analyzes them. In a risk analysis, the risk situ-
ation is represented using different configurable risk matrixes. The risk analysis can
represent the actual or target analysis. Each risk matrix cell shows the number of
causes with their respective valuations.
The risk analysis is based on the following valuation categories:
 Probability of occurrence at the level of preventive actions or directly at the level of
the cause
 Probability of detection at the level of detection actions
 Severity at the level of the effects
You can combine the risk of these three categories in different risk matrixes. From the
valuation, the following results are determined:
 Classification in each risk matrix.
 Classification of each cause by the risk matrixes that are assigned to the risk analysis
profile used with the following classifications: 0 (green), 1 (yellow), 2 (red). These
assignments are made during configuration.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
732
A combined risk value can be calculated for a cause that was classified in different
matrixes. The risk value is derived by adding the different matrixes together.
Example
If, for example, a cause was classified in three matrixes, where it has one each of the
classifications yellow (1), green (0), and red (2), the total risk is 1 + 0 + 2 = 3. The total risk
provides information about which general risk a cause has. You specify whether a
matrix is used to calculate the total risk.
When you start the FMEA Monitor, you can select one or more FMEAs for which you
want to start the risk analysis. You then choose the Risk Analysis button. A dialog box
appears in which you can specify the risk analysis profile. The risk analysis is displayed
according to the settings. You can switch between the target and actual analysis (see
Figure 16.58).
Figure 16.58 Standard Risk Analysis Profile in the FMEA Monitor
If you choose a cell in a matrix that shows several classified causes, the corresponding
causes can be further selected in the table. In reverse, you can use the table to show the
position of certain causes in the matrixes. To do this, select the causes in the table, and
choose Select in Matrix in the Display column.
In the FMEA Cockpit, you open the risk analysis by selecting an FMEA and choosing Risk
Analysis in the context menu. With Risk Analysis with Lower-Level Elements, you can
specify that all lower-level FMEAs are also included in the risk analysis (see Figure
16.58).
© 

733

16.7 Control Plan
Figure 16.59 shows a risk matrix using the action priority profile as defined in configu-
ration with focus on severity, reflected by the 1 (with the severity in the range of 9-10)

16.7 Control Plan
A control plan is a specific and actionable plan that the business process owner can put
in place to ensure product or process improvements, and it’s the direct outcome of
FMEA. A control plan enables the company to have a working plan in place to avoid
occurrences of failure in the first place, as well as prevent it by taking necessary reac-
tionary steps if it does occur. The control plan and its integration with FMEA enables
companies to have a comprehensive compliance road amap to meet agreed-upon
product or service quality standards. It also includes reactionary steps to take in case of
deviations to the agreed-upon quality standards.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
734
The ability to create a control plan and then integrate it with FMEA in the SAP S/4HANA
system provides the added leverage of having all the critical prevention, detection, and
reactionary information in one system (the SAP system).
To create a control plan, use Transaction QPCP or menu path Logistics  Quality
Management  Quality Planning  Control Plan  Cockpit. Figure 16.60 shows the initial
screen to create a new control plan. You can use a previously created control plan as a
template to create a new control plan. This is possible when you enter the previously
created control plan in the template area. This option enables the system to copy pre-
viously entered information into the new control plan, saving you time and effort with
data entry.
Figure 16.60 Creating a Control Plan
In Figure 16.60, enter the Control Plan “CP-REVO” at the top of the screen, and then
select an available Plan Type, such as Prototype, Prelaunch, or Production, from the

Figure 16.61 shows the Basic Data tab of control plan CP-REVO. Enter the name of the
control plan in the Short Text field, and enter Material “FG129” and Plant “1710”. Enter-
ing a relevant short text to denote what the control plan refers to or is about helps in
identification. For example, a control plan code such as 500 doesn’t help in identifying
or clarifying what it refers to, but a short text such as “REVO (Brake Assembly)” for a
control plan helps the process owner to quickly find it in the search function. Notice
that when you’re creating a control plan, the system sets the status as In Process as
shown in Figure 16.62 (this is the lower half of the screen in Figure 16.61).

again later, once we release the control plan.

16.8 Configuration Basics: FMEA and Control Plan
Figure 16.70 shows both successful FMEA integration with the control plan and the fact
that the structure contains the requisite characteristics. These two are shown with two
green lights. Figure 16.71 shows FMEA REVO (Transaction QM_FMEA), in which we
chose the CP (control plan) tab. The system successfully integrates FMEA REVO with
control plan CP-REVO.
Figure 16.71 Integration of Control Plan CP-REVO with FMEA REVO
16.8 Configuration Basics: FMEA and Control Plan
The standard objects that SAP delivers for FMEA are generally sufficient to let compa-
nies immediately put FMEA to work. At the same time, additional available configura-
tion options facilitate meeting specific requirements or unique business needs of
companies.
In this section, we’ll cover some of the important FMEA configuration objects, the busi-
ness processes of which were comprehensively discussed and covered in this chapter.
It was important to first understand the business processes in the SAP S/4HANA sys-
tem before delving into customizing them to meet your company’s needs.
Tips and Tricks
To save you the effort of defining all the parameters in any configuration object, and
also lessen the chances of errors, we suggest that you copy it from one of the standard
available objects and then make the desired changes to the newly created object. The
copy function is available in all configuration objects. Look for the Copy As option.

sections.title: Field Selection
sections.text:
16.8.1 Field Selection
To a large extent, the process owner can control the fields that the user must enter or
that are only available for display. For example, at the time of creating a new FMEA
structure in the system, if you want the business process owner to enter the Minimum
Result field in FMEA, then you can control it to make it a required field for data entry.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
742
Apart from the required option, you can control fields for input, display only, or high-
light, and even hide fields that aren’t relevant or have no user intervention or input.
To set up or control field selection in FMEA, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage-
ment  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  System Modifi-
cation  Field Selection. A popup appears in which you can select from one of three field
groups. These field groups are list items (SAPPLM_FMEA_LISTITEM), actions (SAPPLM_
FMEA_ACTION), and FMEAs (SAPPLM_FMEA). For this example, select SAPPLM_FMEA.
In Figure 16.72, for example, you can make the Minimum Result field required by choos-
ing the Req. (required) radio button.
Figure 16.72 Field Selection

sections.title: Valuation Specification
sections.text:
16.8.2 Valuation Specification
The system refers to the valuation specification to valuate a code that the user enters
for a specific occurrence, severity, and detection. This code, together with its values,
forms the basis for calculating RPN. You define valuation specifications of not just the
severity and occurrence but also detection.
To set up a valuation profile in FMEA, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management 
Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  Lists  Valuation Spec-
ifications. Figure 16.73 shows the initial view of a valuation profile that consists of sev-
eral valuation profiles, including severity, detection, and occurrences.
© 

743
16.8 Configuration Basics: FMEA and Control Plan
Choose Valuation Profile 8000 in Figure 16.73, and then choose Valuation from the left
side, and Figure 16.74 appears. Here, you can define the valuation codes, together with
their descriptions and valuation points of individual codes. Select the Valuation Pro-
posal checkbox if you want the system to propose valuation when you choose a spe-
cific valuation code.
Figure 16.73 Valuation Profile in FMEA
Figure 16.74 Details of Valuation Profile 8000

sections.title: Structure of Question List
sections.text:
16.8.3 Structure of Question List
Just like the FMEA structure, you can also set up a structure for a question list. This will
help you define the questions and any associated hierarchy. For example, at the first
level, you can define a question list and then define whether they’re FMEA questions or
audit questions. To set up the structure of a question list in FMEA, follow menu path

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
744
SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analy-
sis (FMEA)  Lists  Structure of List of Questions. Figure 16.75 shows how you can set up
a question list in a structured form and assign an item type to it.
Figure 16.75 Profile for Hierarchy Levels in Question List

sections.title: Priorities
sections.text:
16.8.4 Priorities
Priorities belong to question lists and questions within the question list. A priority
defines how important it is for the company to get satisfactory and comprehensive
answers to the questions that are critical to the success of the FMEA initiative. To set up
the priority of each question, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspec-
tion Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  Lists  Priorities (see Figure
16.76).
Figure 16.76 Priorities
©

16.8 Configuration Basics: FMEA and Control Plan

sections.title: List Structure
sections.text:
16.8.5 List Structure
The system provides the flexibility to set up the FMEA hierarchy to meet the com-
pany’s business needs or fall more in line with the company’s specific business pro-
cesses. For example, in FMEA, you can first record an effect that has resulted from a
defect (failure mode) and then accordingly find out the cause of the defect. This exam-
ple is specifically applicable when you want to implement process improvements
using FMEA. However, the approach (and the example) just discussed deviates from the
established FMEA business processes, in which you first record a defect, find out the
cause for it, and finally evaluate how the defect will have an effect on a product or pro-
cess before you set up detection and preventive actions. In addition, in this step, you
assign the valuation profile that you’ve defined in Section 16.8.2.
To set up a profile for hierarchy levels in FMEA, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality
Management  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  Lists 
List Structure. Figure 16.77 consists of available standard profiles. In this chapter, and
for this example, we’ve used Hierarchy Level 80 and its associated items. Choose Hier-
archy 80 with the hierarchy profile function in Figure 16.77, and Figure 16.78 appears. In
Figure 16.77, you can define the hierarchy levels, together with a description and
whether a specific hierarchy level has a valuation. Where there’s a valuation, you assign
the Valuation Profile; otherwise, deselect the checkbox under the No Valuation col-
umn. Notice the Item Type column, which enables you to choose the available FMEA
item types, such as prerequisites, characteristics, failure modes, and reasons.
Figure 16.77 Profile for Hierarchy Levels in FMEA

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
746
Figure 16.78 Details of Hierarchy Profile
Tips and Tricks
Here’s a quick way to determine a specific item type within FMEA. In the FMEA Cockpit
(Transaction QM_FMEA), choose the Administration tab, and in the Technical Data
area, you’ll find the Item Type of the specific FMEA item, such as a characteristic or
detection action.

sections.title: Rating Profile
sections.text:
16.8.6 Rating Profile
Before the system calculates the RPN for FMEA, it asks the business process owner to
assign a rating profile. A rating profile refers to a predefined segregation to valuate
whether the RPN value should evaluate the FMEA as, for example, low risk, high risk, or
no risk at all. Refer to Figure 16.40, where we assigned a rating profile before proceeding
to calculate the RPN.
To set up a rating profile, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection
Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition  Rating (see
Figure 16.79).
Figure 16.79 Available Rating Profile
© 

747
16.8 Configuration Basics: FMEA and Control Plan
Here, you can assign a rating profile and give it a short description. Choose Rating Pro-
file 50 in Figure 16.79, and then choose Rating from the left side of the screen. In Figure
16.80, you can define the percentage based on which the system assigns a rating code
to an FMEA after it calculates the RPN. It shows that the RPN having a percentage rating
between 80.0% and 95.0% enables the system to assign the FMEA as Minor Improve-
ments Required in the Rating field (refer to Figure 16.41 again).
Figure 16.80 Details of the Rating Profile
Tips and Tricks
Figure 16.80 shows the configuration settings for Rating Profile. This is the same rating
profile we used in the FMEA calculation. For FMEA results from 66% to 100%, we
defined that the FMEA is rated as No Risk. Similarly, FMEA results from 0% (blank field)
to 33% should be categorized as High Risk.
To set up a rating profile to meet your company’s business needs in FMEA, use menu
path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects
Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition  Rating.

sections.title: FMEA Type
sections.text:
16.8.7 FMEA Type
When setting up an FMEA, one of the first pieces of information that the system
requires from the business process owner is the FMEA type. An FMEA type can be a sys-
tem, product, process, or other. You can also define an FMEA type to meet your com-
pany’s needs. However, note that with every FMEA type, you also have to assign it an
FMEA category (system, product, process, or other).
To set up an FMEA type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection
Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition  FMEA Types (see
Figure 16.81). Here, you see FMEA type 81 with the FMEA category 3 process. You can
define the calculation procedure, such as RPN or absolute deviation, as a value or a per-
centage. Further, you can also define the minimum result of the procedure. Choose
Entry Fields for FMEA Type (on the left side) in Figure 16.81, and Figure 16.82 appears.

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan
748
Figure 16.81 FMEA Type
Figure 16.82 Entry Fields for FMEA Type
In Figure 16.82, you can assign the table and the field name within the table so that that
it becomes available at the time of creating the FMEA. Here, table MARA and the field
name MATNR enable the business process owner to select material from the dropdown
list while creating the FMEA.
Choose Settings for Roles in Figure 16.82. This screen enables you to define the roles
that will let you control who can be part of the FMEA initiative. The roles that you
assign here are then available in the Participants(s) tab of FMEA items.
For the last item in this screen (Digital Signature), refer to Chapter 3, Section 3.2.3.

sections.title: Objects, Properties, and Forms
sections.text:
16.8.8 Objects, Properties, and Forms
SAP delivers standard ABAP objects, such as forms and scripts, for FMEA. In fact, the
output/forms that you saw in preventive and detection actions, as well as those of the
question list, were all standard, SAP-delivered ABAP objects. You can engage an ABAP
resource to custom-develop ABAP objects to meet your company’s business needs and
then assign the same in this step.
To assign already developed ABAP objects, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Manage-
ment  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition 
Control Data  Data Objects, Properties, Forms (see Figure 16.83). Here, you have the
option to assign Smart Forms or Adobe Forms to object types, such as FMEA, the question
list, or corrective/preventive actions. For Adobe Forms, you need to ensure that ADS is
already installed in your SAP S/4HANA system.
Figure 16.83 Data Objects

sections.title: Control Plan Type
sections.text:
16.8.9 Control Plan Type
Just like the FMEA type, you can also set up a new control plan type if the ones that SAP
delivers don’t meet your company’s business needs. To set up a control plan type, use
menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection Planning  Failure Mode and
Effects Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition  Control Plan  Define Control Plan Types. In
Figure 16.84, you can define a new control plan type and assign it a plan phase, such as
Production, Prototype, or Prelaunch. Here, you also assign an ABAP object (Form), such
as a Smart Form or Adobe Form, to the control plan type.
Figure 16.84 Control Plan Type

16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan

sections.text:
16.8.10 Structure Type in Control Plan
Structure types in control plans enable you to control the information and options avail-
able to business process owners at the time of creating a control plan. To set up a struc-
ture type in the control plan, use menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Inspection
Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)  FMEA Definition  Control Plan 
Define Structure Types. In Figure 16.85, you can create a structure type and perform the
steps in all the objects available on the left side of the screen. Choose structure type 0002
in Figure 16.85 and then Object Type on the left side to get to Figure 16.86.
Figure 16.86 appears when you choose structure type 002, object type 1 for material,
process type 2 for production, and finally object 2.

16.9 Summary
In this chapter, you learned how to map real-world FMEA processes and implement
them in the QM area of the SAP S/4HANA system. The chapter covered the three
important factors that make up the RPN. The FMEA Monitor, the risk monitor, creating
a control plan, and its integration with FMEA were also discussed in detail.
The next chapter discusses Early Warning System (EWS).
